errors.claim: Income per head first pulled ahead in the north-west after the Black Death, roughly 1350-1500 ... Industry made the gap huge after 1800, but it did not start it.
errors.fix: Sustained income growth is mainly a post-1800 story; pre-1800 gains were small and reversible. The answer frames a 1350 start with too much confidence and underplays this.

errors.claim: Real wages roughly rose by half or more in a few decades
errors.fix: Real wages rose substantially, but the size varies by series and region. 'Half or more' is stated too firmly.

errors.claim: Milan (2.5 million) and Prague (910,000) in 1800 in the index
errors.fix: These are index artefacts; the answer flags them as suspect, but Antwerp at 591,000 in 1800 is also implausible (about 60,000) and is not flagged.

errors.claim: The Little Ice Age (c.1300-1850) ... the rich northwest withstood it better ... plague in Naples in 1656 helped drag the south down
errors.fix: This causal link between plague and southern decline is contested and leans on Pamuk; it is presented with limited hedging.

grade.best: It uses a population-versus-income distinction and the Maddison series to show that medieval growth was in headcount while the post-plague rise in income per head persisted, and it names the Pomeranz and Allen debate.
grade.worst: State plainly that sustained income growth is mainly post-1800 and that the pre-1800 gains were small and reversible, instead of framing the post-1348 rise as the clear start; coal and Atlantic trade as causes also need fuller treatment.

errors.claim: The Sui dynasty joined the Grand Canal 'from Hangzhou toward Luoyang and later Beijing' and 'After the Tang fell in 907, a Kaifeng and Hangzhou linked by that canal'; Song capital Kaifeng sat on it
errors.fix: Broadly correct; but the 'over 1,700 km' figure is the later Ming-Qing form, which the answer flags as approximate. Not a real error.

errors.claim: Mongols 'brought back state examinations in 1315' and Kumarajiva 'translated the Lotus Sutra into Chinese in Xi'an in 406'
errors.fix: Both are essentially correct (Yuan exams revived 1315; Kumarajiva translated in Chang'an in 406). No error.

errors.claim: Fei River 383: 'kept China divided for two more centuries' and 'Western Jin absorbed Cao Wei's land' in 265 'briefly rejoined the pieces', listed as step on the Fei River logic
errors.fix: Western Jin took over Wei in 265 but unified China only in 280 after conquering Wu; presenting 265 as rejoining pieces is imprecise.

errors.claim: Frame lists fractures at 220, 316, 907, 1127, 1279 CE and says China reunified 'each time'; 1279 is a reunification, not a fracture
errors.fix: 1279 is the Yuan reunification; fractures were roughly 220, 316, 907, 1127. Also, Southern Song/Jin split in 1127 was not followed by native reunification before the Mongols.

errors.claim: Unity 'cheap' because the plain has no internal wall, and the Yangtze 'stopped the north from reuniting China' at Red Cliffs, suggesting a 'steppe-fed army' of Cao Cao
errors.fix: Cao Cao's army was largely northern Han infantry; 'steppe-fed' is loose. Minor.

grade.best: It layers geography (open plain plus canal), a copyable Qin-Han institutional template, exams and the Mandate into a linked causal chain, and honestly shows how rivers sustained division.
grade.worst: It never states the Ko-Koyama-Sng steppe-threat mechanism explicitly, and it leaves the long 220-589 and Five Dynasties divisions underexplained as a counterweight to the 'unity as default' claim.

errors.claim: The Maurya hold lasted about 140 years as the first time one center reached both cores, with the Thar Desert pushing the Indus and Ganges systems apart and Delhi in the gap (minor geography framing); and 'Muhammad bin Tughluq ... token coinage' placed with Daulatabad moved in 1327 and abandoned 'within years'
errors.fix: Daulatabad was made a second capital c.1327 and abandoned c.1335; this is roughly right, so not a real error. The more real slip: 'Tughlaq Dynasty hit 2.449 Mkm² in 1333, the closest India came to unity before the Mughals' understates Alauddin Khalji's and Maurya/Gupta reach, and Tughluq's reach is generally rated as covering most of the subcontinent

errors.claim: Bahmani Sultanate founded 'that year' (1348) in step 12, versus 1347 in steps 9 and 6
errors.fix: Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347; the answer is internally inconsistent

errors.claim: Vijayanagara dated 1344 to 1571 in step 12 versus founded 1336 elsewhere
errors.fix: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 and lasted to c.1646 (the Aravidu dynasty); the 1344-1571 dates are inconsistent and wrong

errors.claim: The north 'is the exception that can be conquered whole' / 'the south never needed the north'; and that Mughals 'held both passes by 1707'
errors.fix: The Mughals lost Kandahar and Kabul-side control was contested, and Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739; holding both passes by 1707 is overstated

grade.best: It builds a clear, multi-layered causal chain linking separate granary cores, grain transport costs, sea trade and overlordship ideology to explain why even the Maurya, Tughlaq and Mughal empires dissolved.
grade.worst: It omits the armed peasantry and open military labour market (Kolff) as a cause of cheap rebellion, and it has inconsistent dates (Bahmani 1347 vs 1348, Vijayanagara 1336 vs 1344) and an overstated claim that the Tughlaq reach was the nearest to unity.

errors.claim: Mycenaean Greece ended by 1101 BCE (stated in the short answer as the collapse date, and in step 12)
errors.fix: The Mycenaean palaces were destroyed around 1200-1180 BCE; 1101 is an Atlas end-date convention, not the palace collapse, and it conflicts with the answer's own 'within a few decades' framing.

errors.claim: Ugarit's last king Ammurapi wrote that the Hittite overlord demanded ships and troops while 'Ugarit's fleet is far away' in Hatti, and that Ugarit's fleet was 'away in Hatti' (step 8) at the time of the 1177 battles
errors.fix: The ships-in-Lycia/Hatti letter (RS 20.238) is real but the exact framing is loose; the Ugarit letters are dated before the destruction around 1185, not tied to the 1177 battles.

errors.claim: Nur Sherif and Amiet-style storm-of-quakes ideas
errors.fix: The earthquake storm hypothesis is by Amos Nur and Eric Cline; 'Nur Sherif' and 'Amiet' are spurious attributions.

grade.best: It frames the collapse as a cascading systems failure, linking drought, the tin trade, palace centralisation and vassal obligations, and weighs Cline, Kaniewski, Nur and Cline, and Drews fairly.
grade.worst: Clean up the dating and attribution slips (Mycenaean end at 1101, the 'Nur Sherif and Amiet' garble) and say plainly that the collapse ran over decades and not in the year 1177.

errors.claim: The Temple of Artemis ended in 401 CE by Christian-era dismantling; Chrysostom's campaign was the last blow, with no mention of Herostratus's 356 BCE arson
errors.fix: Herostratus burned it in 356 BCE; it was rebuilt, then wrecked by Goths in 268 CE (answer gives 262 and omits the rebuild)

errors.claim: Mausoleum: Knights began Bodrum Castle in 1406 (or 1402) and in 1522 the site was taken apart after their surrender at Rhodes; the answer also says Knights quarried it in 1522
errors.fix: Knights began Bodrum Castle in 1402 and reused the stone then; in 1522 they lost Rhodes, not Bodrum. Dates are inconsistent across steps

errors.claim: The Colossus of Rhodes is placed among wonders on an 'Aegean western Anatolian fault zone' and the Library of Alexandria is treated alongside the Seven Wonders
errors.fix: The Library was never one of the Seven Wonders; this is a digression, not a core error

errors.claim: Babylon's walls sometimes replaced the Lighthouse in earliest lists
errors.fix: Walls of Babylon sometimes appear in lists, but the Lighthouse is normally the replacement for them (or Ishtar Gate) in later lists, so this is reversed or at best unclear

grade.best: It gives a clear, causal account of why each wonder ended (earthquakes, law and belief, lack of upkeep) and names Dalley's Nineveh hypothesis with honest uncertainty about the Hanging Gardens.
grade.worst: Fix the Temple of Artemis account (Herostratus 356 BCE, rebuilt, Goths 268 CE) and make the Bodrum Castle dates consistent, since these are inconsistent or missing.

errors.claim: Constantine introduced the gold solidus around 309 ... for roughly 700 years it kept its weight
errors.fix: The solidus was introduced c. 309-312 but its fineness was debased from the 11th century (Alexios I's reforms ca. 1092 replaced it with the hyperpyron); the weight/purity record holds roughly 700 years only loosely.

errors.claim: The Theodosian Walls ... were rebuilt in 447 within about two months ... as 'cheap to build because the site did most of the work'; and 'Theodosian Walls, a triple line over 5 km long'
errors.fix: The walls were first built 413 and repaired in 447 after the earthquake; the claim that they were cheap because of the site is an unsupported inference, though not seriously wrong.

errors.claim: In 410 Rome itself was sacked by Visigoths, 'the first fall of the city in 800 years'
errors.fix: Correct in outline (since the Gauls c. 390 BCE), but the Atlas says West 'fragility' of 'Western Roman Empire (395-475)' and others; no major error here.

errors.claim: The East was Constantinople's Hunnic tribute 'roughly 2,100 pounds of gold a year late in Attila's reign' and the East 'paid gold to Attila and thereby steered him elsewhere'
errors.fix: The tribute (700 lb, raised to 2,100 lb in 447) was paid by the East, but Attila turned west in 451 for his own reasons (Honoria's claim, Marcian ending tribute), not because he was steered by payment.

errors.claim: In 1204 'Walls fell only to treachery of a different kind' and the 1348 city of 'perhaps 50,000'
errors.fix: The 1204 capture was by assault from the Golden Horn sea walls, not strictly treachery; population estimate is plausible but uncertain.

errors.claim: Constantinople fell in 1453 to 'Ottoman guns, not geography, broke the Theodosian wall'
errors.fix: Largely right, but the city also fell because it had only about 7,000 defenders; fine.

grade.best: It links geography, a gold-backed fiscal base and the military-political structure (generals controlling emperors in the West, civil officials in the East) into a coherent comparison with explicit cross-links and honest limits.
grade.worst: It never questions the framing that Rome 'fell' in 476 as an event rather than a gradual dissolution into successor kingdoms, and it overlooks the continuity/accommodation schools (Brown, Goffart).

errors.claim: Step 8 heading and text: 'Florence loses a third, Cologne gains a sixth' alongside 'usual estimate is that Florence lost roughly half to three-fifths'
errors.fix: Heading contradicts body; Florence is usually put at roughly half or more lost, not a third.

errors.claim: Step 6: plague crossed the Alps by the Brenner toward Vienna and reached the Danube; Bohemia and Poland described as lightly hit as established pattern
errors.fix: Spread into central Europe is poorly documented; the Brenner route claim is shaky, and light impact in Bohemia/Poland is contested (stated hedged).

errors.claim: Step 12: serfdom 'tightened later' in the East because of a 'smaller post-plague labor shock'
errors.fix: The second serfdom is usually tied to lord power and later commercial grain demand, not mainly a smaller labor shock; the answer partly hedges this.

grade.best: It traces the route step by step from the Chu valley to Caffa, then Messina and Marseille, hedges the rat and flea question, and links famine, trade, mortality and wage effects.
grade.worst: It never mentions the massacres of Jews blamed for the plague (Strasbourg 1349), and it gives only a vague, hedged account of serfdom weakening in the west and a second serfdom in the east.

errors.claim: Babylon, 100 km north on the Euphrates at the point where it comes closest to the Tigris, survived from 2300 BCE to 100 CE
errors.fix: Babylon is about 85-100 km south of Baghdad, in central Mesopotamia and north of Ur and Uruk; calling it 'north' of Ur is fine, but its decline was long and political, and describing it as vanishing at 100 CE is a simplification of a city that persisted as a town into the Islamic era.

errors.claim: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had the same weakness: monsoon-fed rivers like the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra shift course
errors.fix: The Ghaggar-Hakra link is contested, and the answer flags this only partly; it presents river shifting as the mechanism in the main text.

errors.claim: Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE yet rebuilt... it only fades in 698 CE when Tunis and Kairouan take over
errors.fix: Broadly correct, but Carthage is listed as a city that 'faded' in the frame while the step shows it persisting for centuries; the framing is inconsistent.

errors.claim: Ur's final abandonment around 450 BCE came as the river moved and the head of the Persian Gulf coast changed
errors.fix: The Euphrates shift is plausible for Ur, but the Gulf coastline change is debated and was not the cause of abandonment; it is stated too confidently.

errors.claim: Jerusalem was a long-lived city but Babylon 'had everything a city needs' and its sacred role was tied to a king and temple, so it ended 100 CE
errors.fix: Babylon's decline was gradual and linked to Seleucid Seleucia, Ctesiphon and shifting politics; the sacred-role explanation is speculative.

grade.best: It turns the lists into explanatory mechanisms (single channel, single toll commodity, maintenance-heavy network versus chokepoint plus fallback income) and tests them against counterexamples like Jerusalem.
grade.worst: Tighten factual claims about Ur's coastline, Babylon's end date and Carthage's mixed fate, and cite Bosker and Buringh or Jane Jacobs to give the scholarly debate on why cities persist.

errors.claim: The Americas lost perhaps 80 to 90 percent of their people (stated in the short answer and frame as 'killing most Native Americans' / 'emptied')
errors.fix: The 80-90% figure is a high-end estimate that depends on contested pre-contact numbers; the rubric says by most estimates well over half. The answer hedges in the short answer, so this is a minor overstatement.

errors.claim: Africa's population stagnated at around 100 million across the 1700s while the rest of the world grew
errors.fix: The figure is a rough, contested estimate (Manning's), presented fairly firmly.

grade.best: It builds a clear causal chain from disease to population collapse to labor shortage to slavery, silver and crops, and states the uncertainty about pre-contact numbers openly, with named scholars (Crosby, Mann, Koch/Lewis and Maslin) and fair for/against views.
grade.worst: Horses, cattle and wheat are barely covered, with no mention of Plains horse cultures, so the Old World animals and crops that transformed the Americas are thin; it should also state the 80-90% loss as a range tied to the contested baseline.

points.cause: Richthofen and the 1877 name appear only in the single-road view; the shifting network is clear in short and step 1-2
Sogdians named as middlemen but not given a first-millennium emphasis
The Mongol peace is covered in depth, but mostly as a plague corridor rather than as reviving overland trade

errors.claim: Taklamakan 'roughly 1,000 km long'; Zhang Qian 'found the Parthians and the Sogdian cities of Samarkand and Merv'
errors.fix: Zhang Qian reached Sogdiana/Ferghana and Bactria; Merv was a Parthian city and he did not visit it. The wording is loose, not clearly wrong.

errors.claim: Paper went from Luoyang 105, Samarkand 751 ... 'about 1,150 years from China to Italy' and moved 'at merchant and administrator speed'
errors.fix: 105 to 1276 is about 1,170 years, so this is only rounding. The wording is fine.

grade.best: It shows how geography (the Taklamakan, passes, steppe against sea) produces a braided relay network, and uses Hansen's relay model to explain why paper, religion and know-how mattered more than luxuries.
grade.worst: Name Richthofen's 1877 coinage in the main answer and give the Sogdians their central first-millennium role, and treat the Mongol peace as reviving trade rather than mainly as a plague corridor.

errors.claim: the steamship had cut the Atlantic crossing to about a week, shorter than the flu's 2-day incubation plus 1 week of illness would need to outlast
errors.fix: The logic is garbled: a week-long crossing is comparable to or longer than the flu's incubation plus infectious period, and troopship crossings took roughly 8-12 days. Ships did carry active outbreaks, but the stated reasoning is confused.

errors.claim: Chandra, Kuljanin and Wray, 'Mortality from the influenza pandemic of 1918-19 in Indonesia', Population Studies, 2012 (cited in the VIEW on India)
errors.fix: The 2012 Demography paper by Chandra, Kuljanin and Wray is 'Reassessing the Indian 1918 Influenza Pandemic'; the Indonesia paper is a different work, so this citation is mismatched.

errors.claim: The virus came with returning soldiers and sailors to Bombay in late May and again in September 1918, and Step 3 says the virus arrived in Bombay by ship in June 1918
errors.fix: Bombay's first cases are usually dated to late May-June 1918, and the two steps give inconsistent dates and details; the deadly second wave reached Bombay in September.

errors.claim: The Atlas's Maddison series shows the toll: India's population stagnated, ... when about 8 million a year of normal growth would have been expected
errors.fix: Pre-1920 Indian population growth was well under that rate, so the 8 million per year baseline is overstated, and Maddison figures cannot isolate flu deaths.

grade.best: It builds a layered causal chain (wartime troop and ship logistics, censorship, a short infectious period, then thin states and hunger) and backs it with the Samoa vs American Samoa natural experiment.
grade.worst: Fix the inconsistent details (the garbled steamship-timing logic, the mismatched Chandra citation, the unreliable Maddison baseline) and state the young-adult W-shaped mortality curve explicitly rather than only in passing.

errors.claim: Step 1 says the Mozambique Channel offered no reliable return wind, explaining why Kilwa, not Great Zimbabwe's coast, became the gold exit (Great Zimbabwe 'coast' is not a thing; Sofala was the gold port, and Kilwa controlled Sofala only later).
errors.fix: Sofala was the main gold outlet; Kilwa dominated it by controlling the Sofala trade from the 13th-14th century. Monsoon limits explain the southern reach of Swahili towns, not a lack of return winds in the Channel.

errors.claim: Step 9 says Srivijaya 'in the index until 1377' and step 10 says it lasted 674 to 1293 CE; also step 12 says the Mamluk Sultanate 1241-1518 while other steps say 1250-1517.
errors.fix: Dates are inconsistent across steps; Mamluk Sultanate is usually 1250-1517.

errors.claim: Step 4 says the summer southwest monsoon carried ships east to India and the winter northeast monsoon brought them home.
errors.fix: This reverses the usual pattern for the western ocean: the southwest monsoon (April-August) carried ships from Arabia/Africa to India, and the northeast monsoon (Nov-March) carried them back west. Step 4 is correct on the first half but conflicts with Step 1 on Africa; the 'brought them home' framing is ambiguous. Step 11 has cargo arriving at Aden on the southwest monsoon, which is wrong direction for goods from India to Aden (they came on the northeast monsoon).

errors.claim: Step 10 says Ships from China waited for the northeast wind to go home and southwest to return.
errors.fix: In the South China Sea the northeast monsoon carries ships south to Southeast Asia and the southwest monsoon carries them north to China, so the directions are reversed.

grade.best: It turns the wind calendar into a causal chain from one round trip a year to waiting, to ports, credit, diasporas and tolls, with honest labelling of what is inferred.
grade.worst: Fix the monsoon direction errors (Step 11 and Step 10) and add the classical Red Sea to Muziris route and the 1498 da Gama arrival with the Portuguese attempt to control trade by force.

errors.claim: Britain alone carried perhaps 3 million people, a bit over a quarter of all embarked
errors.fix: Britain carried roughly 3.2 million, about 26% of the 12.5 million, so this is roughly correct; Portugal/Brazil carried the most (about 5.8 million). Not a real error.

grade.best: It gives the SlaveVoyages totals and the destination split clearly, then explains them through winds, sugar and mining demand, and state licensing, while stating that Brazil and the Caribbean, not the US, took most captives.
grade.worst: It never says that the trade peaked in the 18th century. A clear statement of the peak, with its numbers, would complete the sugar-driven causal story.

errors.claim: Musa's 1324 hajj ran roughly 6,000 km or more each way from the Niger bend through the desert to Cairo and on to Mecca
errors.fix: Niger bend to Cairo is roughly 4,500 to 5,000 km by caravan routes; about 6,000 km is an overstatement for that leg, though the total to Mecca is larger. Flagged as the answer's own estimate.

errors.claim: Musa's realm was 'bigger than anything in the Atlas's window except Mamluk Egypt and the Byzantines'
errors.fix: Mali's territory was very large, and the Byzantine Empire in 1324 was a small remnant state, far smaller than Mali. The comparison is wrong.

errors.claim: The Kouroukan Fouga is dated 1236 and the answer says 'Sundiata's heirs inherited' it as a constitution-like charter
errors.fix: Tradition attributes the charter to Sundiata himself at the time of founding (c. 1235-36), so it was not inherited by his heirs.

grade.best: It explains wealth as a toll-and-rationing system on the gold and salt trade, links it to Musa's Cairo spending and the Catalan Atlas image, and flags the second-hand nature of the figures.
grade.worst: Give Timbuktu and Djenne clearly as trade and learning centres in the wealth argument, and drop the Black Death digressions and the wrong claim about Mali's size relative to Byzantium.

points.where_note: jiaozi and commerce covered; Champa rice not mentioned

errors.claim: Hartwell iron output of 125,000 tonnes is 'of the same order as Europe's total output many centuries later'; also roughly 1 kg per person
errors.fix: Hartwell's figure is often compared to Britain's output c. 1788 (~76,000 tonnes) or Europe's c. 1700; 125,000 t over ~100 million people is ~1.2 kg, acceptable, but the comparison is vague and arguably loose

errors.claim: Caishi 1161: Wanyan Liang was killed by his own officers, and the Song fleet used gunpowder weapons; Mongols' Xiangyang fell 1273 after 'Persian counterweight trebuchets'
errors.fix: Broadly correct; no clear error here

errors.claim: The 1005 Chanyuan treaty paid Liao roughly 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year
errors.fix: The treaty set 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk; correct per many sources (some say 200,000 taels initially in later 1042 raised). Minor

errors.claim: Song shows 'the Yuan (1294 onward...)' and 'examinations suspended for decades, resuming in 1315'; 'UK GDP per capita near 1,100 to 1,500 dollars across 1268-1368' used to weigh Song
errors.fix: Yuan was proclaimed in 1271 (Kublai), not 1294; the UK GDP data are irrelevant to Song China's comparison

errors.claim: The Song 'lost the northern coal-iron belt' and that southern China lacked coal-iron near markets, with Elvin credited for this
errors.fix: The coal/iron-loss thesis is Hartwell's; Elvin's argument is the high-level equilibrium trap, though Elvin does discuss the iron decline. Minor misattribution

grade.best: It ties geography, state fiscal-military demand and the 1127 loss of the northern coal-iron belt into a causal chain, and weighs Elvin, Hartwell, Allen and Pomeranz with clear hedging.
grade.worst: It omits Champa rice and drifts into irrelevant side data (UK GDP, plague) and some loose dating (Yuan 1294), diluting an otherwise strong answer.

errors.claim: Karakorum (founded 1220) sits on the Orkhon; Ögedei built Karakorum (on the map from 1220)
errors.fix: Karakorum was founded around 1220 as a camp, but the city was built under Ögedei in the 1230s. The claim is roughly fine, though the date is loosely handled.

errors.claim: Mongol Empire gains 4.5 million km² in 1220 and 5.5 million km² by 1227
errors.fix: These are model figures from the Atlas, not certain facts. They are presented as map data, so this is only a minor concern.

grade.best: It links steppe grass, the decimal army and keshig, the yam, and calibrated terror into one causal chain, and it flags uncertain claims such as the Yasa text, casualty figures, and the Hungary withdrawal.
grade.worst: It omits the favourable climate evidence (Pederson tree rings, 1211-25) and never states that the empire split into four khanates, or that the Yuan conquered Song China by 1279.

errors.claim: Mehmed built Rumeli Hisarı in 1452, which cut the strait... Anadolu Hisari (1394) and Rumeli Hisari (1452) let Mehmed II cut the Black Sea grain and supply line
errors.fix: Largely correct, but the answer says the Greeks held 'some 20 km of walls' in step 8 versus 6.5 km land front elsewhere; the full circuit is about 20 km, so this is consistent, not an error. No confident factual error here.

errors.claim: Venetian trade shifted so that Ottoman tolls pushed Europeans to the Atlantic route (link step 12 -> step 6)
errors.fix: The answer itself says 1453 was an accelerant at most; Portuguese expansion began in 1415 and spices ran via Mamluk Egypt, so the link line overstates causation.

grade.best: It explains the fall as a mechanism, walls outliving the state, linking lost hinterland, fiscal incapacity to afford Orban's guns, and a thin garrison stretched by the ships hauled into the Golden Horn.
grade.worst: It never says that Greek scholars carried manuscripts to Italy and contributed to the Renaissance, and it gives no figure for Byzantium's tiny population, so two aftermath and rump-state points are only partly covered.

errors.claim: Chan Chan/Chimú capital listed as ending 1470 in one place and the Chimú Empire 1481 in another, with conquest 'around 1470'
errors.fix: Inca conquest of Chimor is usually dated c. 1470, so the 1481 end date is inconsistent; minor internal discrepancy

errors.claim: the Inca empire 'grew roughly 30-fold in about 60 years' and relay runners every 2 to 2.5 km covering ~200 km a day
errors.fix: Chasqui stations were roughly 2.5 km apart in some accounts, and about 240 km per day is the commonly cited figure; the figures are approximate and flagged as estimates, so this is not a real error

grade.best: It explains the mechanism clearly, linking labour tax, qollqa storehouses, khipu counts, roads and mitmaq into one system, and names the unknowns honestly, including whether khipu held narrative.
grade.worst: Rapid expansion under Pachacuti is only implied (polity begins 1438, 30-fold growth), and the 1532 conquest context is spread across steps rather than explained crisply as a civil war after smallpox in the short answer.

errors.claim: Cholula, a Tlaxcalan-adjacent holy city... Cortés's later claim of the Cholula massacre rests partly on her warning of an ambush (framed as Cholula being an Aztec-linked center broken)
errors.fix: Broadly accurate; but the claim that smallpox 'reached Tenochtitlan in 1520' is fine. Minor: Cuitlahuac ruled about 80 days and the smallpox arrived in the Gulf with Narváez's expedition, which is correct. No clear serious error.

errors.claim: Moctezuma II died around 29 June 1520 and Cuitlahuac died of smallpox 'within months' while Texcoco 'came over to Cortés by 1521' as a defection in a cascade caused by his death
errors.fix: Texcoco's ruling faction came over to Cortés in late 1520 / early 1521 under Cortés's influence, and Tlaxcala alliance predated the smallpox; the causal link to Cuitlahuac's death is overstated.

errors.claim: Cortés 'scuttled his ships in 1519' (stated as fact)
errors.fix: Historians dispute this: Cortés had the ships disabled/dismantled (not burned), and Restall treats the 'burned ships' story as a myth.

grade.best: It ties the causes into linked mechanisms (tribute fragility, Tlaxcala as anvil, Malinche's diplomacy, smallpox decapitation, lake siege) and explicitly rejects the Quetzalcoatl myth and the technology-alone explanation.
grade.worst: Tighten a few causal claims (Texcoco's defection tied to Cuitlahuac's death, the 'scuttled ships' detail) and add the allied warrior numbers with firmer sourcing.

errors.claim: Wilhelm, reading Serbia's reply on 28 July, said all reason for war had vanished, but it was too late (listed as after Nicholas's 29-30 July mobilization sequence)
errors.fix: Wilhelm's 'Halt in Belgrade' proposal was real, but Nicholas's 29 July telegram exchange and cancellation are accurately described; no real error beyond compressed chronology. Sazonov was foreign minister, not a general, so calling him one of Nicholas's 'generals' is wrong.

errors.claim: Princip... the driver took a wrong turn onto Franz Josef Street, stalled at Schiller's delicatessen... The first bomb thrown at about 10:10
errors.fix: Broadly correct; Princip was one of a group of conspirators, and Čabrinović's bomb bounced off the car. No material error.

grade.best: It builds a causal chain from Balkan nationalism through blank cheque, ultimatum, mobilisation and Schlieffen timetable, explicitly rejecting automatic war, and weighs Fischer, Clark and Taylor fairly.
grade.worst: It treats the alliance blocs (Entente vs Central Powers) only indirectly, never clearly explaining how the two-bloc system widened the Balkan war, and it misdescribes Sazonov as one of the generals.

errors.claim: Note the Act's occupation rule applied only to coasts, which left the interior open to paper claims.
errors.fix: That is broadly accurate; the effective occupation clause covered coastal annexations. Not an error.

errors.claim: Italian Africa only appears from 1890 and peaks decades later in 1940, with Adwa 1896 being the reason.
errors.fix: Italian Eritrea dates from 1890, before Adwa; Adwa did not explain the timing, and Italy later conquered Ethiopia in 1936.

errors.claim: Leopold II got recognition because Britain and Germany preferred a weak neutral owner of the Congo; the Act's checklist let such claims be made on paper.
errors.fix: Broadly accurate; however the Free State's recognition came through bilateral recognitions, and the Act's effective occupation rule did not cover it. Minor.

errors.claim: Rinderpest likely arrived with Italian army cattle landing at Massawa around 1887 and reached the Cape by 1896-97.
errors.fix: Plausible and commonly cited; no error.

grade.best: It separates the Berlin Conference's procedural role from the real borders made in bilateral treaties, and links technology, disease, finance and diplomacy into one cost-based causal story.
grade.worst: Fix small slips such as the stray 'Charles H. Ford? no' citation and the muddled Italian Africa timing, and say more about how Berlin attendees ruled on Congo atrocities.

points.why: Mentions 1946 elections, League claims and Cabinet Mission, and Jalal view on Jinnah's demand, but never mentions the 1940 Lahore Resolution or the Pakistan demand explicitly as a demand after failed talks.
Mountbatten arrived March 1947, announced 15 August handover on 3 June, earlier plan June 1948.
Radcliffe had about five weeks; lines published 17 August after independence; covers Punjab and Bengal.
About 14.5 million moved; deaths 200,000 to 2 million.

errors.claim: Muslim League won about 425 of 495 Muslim reserved seats
errors.fix: The League won about 425 of 492 Muslim seats; this is roughly right, so minor and not an error.

errors.claim: Bengal famine killed roughly 2 to 3 million
errors.fix: Most estimates are about 2 to 3 million, with some lower at 1.5 to 2 million; acceptable range, not clearly wrong.

errors.claim: The handover was compressed into ten weeks and Radcliffe 'had about five weeks to draw two commissions' worth of borders'; Direct Action killing in Calcutta put at 'several thousand' in one step and 'about 4,000' in another
errors.fix: Consistent enough; the 3 June to 15 August span is about ten weeks, so no error.

grade.best: It links long-run colonial structures (separate electorates, canal colonies, war strain) to the specific mechanics of the rushed handover, and it weighs Jalal, Khan and Pandey fairly with honest unknowns.
grade.worst: It omits the 1940 Lahore Resolution and Jinnah's explicit Pakistan demand, so the League's side of why partition was demanded is thin.

errors.claim: Zhu Xi relay lands in Edo/Tokyo in 1607 'just as' Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara (1600); Hayashi Razan recruited around 1605
errors.fix: Hayashi Razan entered Ieyasu's service in 1605, but Neo-Confucianism became the shogunate's ideology gradually; Edo was not the 'Tokyo' of 1607 and the relay date is loose. Minor timing looseness.

errors.claim: Roughly 18 to 20 million koku nationwide by the early 1600s, while the shogunate held about 4 million of roughly 30 million koku
errors.fix: The answer contradicts itself; national total was about 18-26 million koku in 1600 rising to about 30 million by the 1700s, and the shogunate held about 4 million.

errors.claim: Source for the Christianity/terauke step: Mikael Adolphson et al., Heian Japan, Centers and Peripheries (2007)
errors.fix: That book is about the Heian period and does not support Tokugawa-era temple registration; the source is mismatched.

grade.best: It builds a real causal chain in which Hideyoshi's disarmament, sankin-kotai, Edo's growth and the Osaka rice market reinforce one another, and it explains the Tokugawa bargain that left the tozama armed.
grade.worst: It should state outright that sakoku was not total closure and tie the end of the peace explicitly to Perry's 1853 arrival and the Meiji Restoration, rather than leaving Perry to a passing unknowns line.

errors.claim: Byzantine-Sasanian war of 603-628 / 26 years of war (602-628) and Ctesiphon fell about 637 with Qadisiyya in 636 fought 'at the desert edge'; Sasanian 'Siege of Ctesiphon 629' in civil war
errors.fix: The war began in 602 (the answer is inconsistent, giving 602, 603); minor date slip, not misleading

errors.claim: The Ghassanids and Lakhmids both end in 633 / had been dismantled by about 602-630
errors.fix: The Lakhmid kingdom ended c. 602 under Khosrow II, and the Ghassanids were weakened around 582 and again after 614-629; neither 'ends in 633' as a clean fact, though the buffers were gone by the conquests

errors.claim: Nahavand in 642 'finished the state, not the war'; Sasanian Empire disappears after 643 in the data
errors.fix: Nahavand was decisive but Yazdegerd III lived until 651, consistent with the 651 end the answer gives elsewhere; small inconsistency

grade.best: It separates fast conquest (exhausted empires, lost buffers, mobile unified Arab armies) from slow conversion (jizya fiscal incentive, garrison towns, Bulliet's curve), and links the two with clear mechanisms.
grade.worst: Tidy the dates and the buffer-kingdom claims (602 vs 603, Ghassanids and Lakhmids ending 'in 633'), and mention the plague of the 540s-740s more directly as a factor instead of leaving it as an unknown.

errors.claim: The iron steamer Nemesis was 'an iron-hulled 2-gun paddle vessel'
errors.fix: Nemesis carried two 32-pounder pivot guns plus other smaller guns and Congreve rocket launchers, so 'notably 2-gun' understates her armament; minor.

errors.claim: Britain's problem was tea: 'a structural drain of silver from Britain toward China' and 'the Atlas has tea reaching London in 1658' as part of the 1790 trade imbalance
errors.fix: Broadly correct, though the Manila and Spanish American silver, not British silver alone, funded most of China's inflow; minor simplification.

errors.claim: In 1841 the Qing counterattacked at Ningpo and Chinhai in early 1842 and failed, 'losing the garrison advantage'; and Chinhai/Ningpo listed as 1841/1842 while the British took them in October 1841
errors.fix: The British captured Chinhai and Ningpo in October 1841; the Qing counterattack on them was in March 1842. The answer's ordering is muddled.

errors.claim: Britain's 'Indian revenue' financed the iron steamer Nemesis and the war, with the claim that 'Britain's India revenue was financed by the very trade Commissioner Lin burned'
errors.fix: Opium revenue was important to the Indian government, but the war was largely funded by the Indian treasury and British government finance; the framing is a loose overstatement.

errors.claim: Chusan fell in July 1840 'after a short bombardment' and 'the Atlas hub relay shows Shanghai taking over from Canton in 1842'
errors.fix: Chusan fell on 5 July 1840 after a brief bombardment, which is correct; Shanghai overtook Canton only gradually after 1843 opening, so 1842 is a rough date.

errors.claim: The British 'never beat the Qing army in a decisive field battle'
errors.fix: British forces did defeat Qing troops in several land engagements, e.g. at Chinkiang, Chinhai and Chapu; the claim is overstated though the strategic point stands.

grade.best: It builds a linked causal chain from opium and silver drain through the Qing's fiscal and informational weakness to steam-enabled strikes on the Yangtze and Grand Canal, and explicitly flags where it goes beyond the data.
grade.worst: It names Platt and Lovell only lightly in the views and does not weigh Platt's revisionist argument that Qing leaders were not inevitably doomed, and a few battle chronology and troop-engagement claims are loose or overstated.

errors.claim: Nalanda was sacked around 1197 (step 10), alongside 'fell around 1200' elsewhere
errors.fix: Nalanda is conventionally dated to c. 1193 (Bakhtiyar Khilji); the answer gives inconsistent dates (1193, 1197, 1200), though within the debated range.

errors.claim: The Tang crackdown 'in the 840s' destroyed monastic estates, yet Chan and Pure Land survived because they needed only a teacher or a name
errors.fix: Broadly right (Huichang 845), but Chan monasteries also held estates and Chan flourished partly under Song state patronage; the portability story is somewhat overstated.

grade.best: It builds a causal chain linking merchant-funded, royal-grant-dependent concentrated monasteries to Hindu absorption and a final blow from the Ghurid raids, and explicitly weighs it against the invasion thesis.
grade.worst: Ashoka's role as the original patron who spread Buddhism outward (missions to Sri Lanka and Central Asia) is treated only as domestic governance, and the East Asian transmission is not tied to him.

errors.claim: Paper reached Europe 1,100 years behind China (Luoyang 105) and Korea (Seoul c.400); Xàtiva 1056
errors.fix: Gap from 105 to Xàtiva 1056 is about 950 years, and the Korea c.400 date is a loose guess; 1,100 years is overstated

errors.claim: Venice 'including Gutenberg's own financier Fust's rivals' went bankrupt; Venice had printed 'some 150 presses' worth of titles'
errors.fix: Muddled and unsupported; Fust was Gutenberg's creditor in Mainz, not a Venetian bankruptcy story

errors.claim: Hangul promulgated 1446 / 1443 and Paris 134,000 in 1234 used as Gutenberg-era Europe; Luoyang 1.7 million and Xi'an 3.1 million in 1234
errors.fix: Atlas model city estimates are inflated; Luoyang/Xi'an were not that large in 1234 and Xi'an was not a Song city

errors.claim: Presses reached Cologne by 1464 (step 5) versus 1465 (step 3); 'Hangul (1443)' versus 1446
errors.fix: Internal inconsistencies in dates

errors.claim: Eisenstein 'says little of Asia' and no mention of Adrian Johns; step 5 says Black Death raised literate craftsmen's share
errors.fix: The Eisenstein-Johns debate is the central historiographical dispute and is omitted; the craftsmen claim is speculative

grade.best: It explains the speed difference through linked mechanisms (alphabet cost, cheap paper, political fragmentation, contested text, state-held type) and refuses to call China slow.
grade.worst: It never names Adrian Johns or the Eisenstein-Johns dispute over how revolutionary print was, and it omits the Ottoman case (Muteferrika 1727), leaving the debate and wider comparison thin.

errors.claim: Beauvais, the tallest choir attempt at about 48 m, fell in 1284 and was never completed. So the Gothic cathedral is a record of a population still expanding, and the plague finishes that record. (Beauvais framed as a result of stalled growth)
errors.fix: Beauvais collapsed in 1284 because of structural overreach, before the Black Death and while population was still high; it was not caused by population stalling.

errors.claim: Notre-Dame was begun c.1163 'when Paris was 124,000' and Paris walled from c.1190 as sign of crowding, with the Atlas figure 124,000 in 1220
errors.fix: Paris in 1220 is commonly estimated at roughly 50,000 or fewer; the 124,000 figure is likely too high, though the answer hedges it.

errors.claim: Sens cathedral begun c.1135-40 and Saint-Denis 'dedicated 1144' with flying buttresses at Notre-Dame c.1180s-1200
errors.fix: Mostly acceptable; flying buttress dating at Notre-Dame is debated, but the claim is hedged.

grade.best: It builds a layered causal account that links Suger's theology of light, structural technology, agrarian surplus, and Capetian politics, and weighs Panofsky, von Simson, and Duby against each other with honest caveats.
grade.worst: Treat the Paris population figure and the Beauvais collapse more carefully: Beauvais was structural overreach in 1284, not a result of demographic stall, and the 124,000 Paris estimate is probably inflated.

points.note: Maragha school and Tusi couple appear only in the Saliba view and the Ibn al-Haytham mention in step 11; Maragha is named, Tusi couple named in view, optics only name-dropped
Copernicus 1543 and Galileo are covered; Newton's Principia (1687) appears only in the frame dates
Printing, autonomous universities and competing states are all covered; Mokyr is cited in step 9, though the Republic of Letters is not named
The answer says the causal weights are thin and a view criticises Needham's framing as hindsight, but it does not state outright that the question itself is contested

errors.claim: Al-Ghazali's Incoherence of the Philosophers (1095) hit the Aristotelian project ... madrasas taught natural philosophy only as a private side-subject
errors.fix: The Incoherence is usually dated c.1095, which is fine, but the framing leans on the discredited 'Ghazali killed science' narrative. The answer partly hedges this by citing Saliba.

errors.claim: Copernicus (1543) and Vesalius (1543) published in Nuremberg and Basel, outside any single censor's reach
errors.fix: Both were printed in the Holy Roman Empire, which is accurate, but Copernicus' printing in Nuremberg was arranged by Rheticus and Osiander. The point about escaping a censor is overstated, since Copernicus was a Catholic canon and the work was dedicated to the Pope.

errors.claim: Galileo left Pisa for Venetian Padua in 1592 and returned to Medici Florence in 1610
errors.fix: Correct as dates, but describing these moves as 'exits' from a censor is a stretch. Galileo moved for pay and patronage, not to escape censorship.

errors.claim: Bi Sheng-era Kaifeng had movable type by 1040
errors.fix: Bi Sheng's type is dated c.1040, but it was in Song China, and the link to Kaifeng is loose. This is a minor imprecision.

grade.best: It rejects 'means or ideas' as the explanation and builds a causal chain through institutional autonomy, political fragmentation and geography, tied to concrete cases such as Paris 1277, Taqi al-Din's observatory and Galileo's moves, while honestly flagging the thin evidence on causal weights.
grade.worst: It should say plainly that the Needham question is a contested framing (hindsight, Eurocentric, and a 'revolution' that arguably continued Islamic work), and develop the Islamic and Chinese achievements (Ibn al-Haytham's optics, the Tusi couple's use by Copernicus) and Newton's Principia, which it barely touches.

errors.claim: Hammurabi's code set penalties; Hittite laws show 'notably more compensation than mutilation' as contrast, and the Corpus was 'written largely in Latin when the East spoke Greek' with Code of 529 'swiftly replaced' (fine) — but 'Tribonian... dismissed after the Nika riot of 532 for corruption and restored by 535 or so'
errors.fix: Tribonian was dismissed in 532 after the Nika riot, and was restored around 535 (fine); no clear error here, but the claim that the Digest was 'in 533' alongside Institutes is accurate.

grade.best: It clearly corrects the 'first code' myth with Ur-Namma and Lipit-Ishtar, and traces a causal arc from king-as-shepherd to debt-driven publication to imperial codification, with candid caveats about enforcement.
grade.worst: It never states that Hammurabi's penalties varied by social class (free man, commoner, slave), a core rubric detail, and gives the Bologna rediscovery only a passing mention without explaining its impact on European civil law.

errors.claim: Greenland colony peaked near 2,000 to 5,000 people; about 25 ships sailed and roughly 14 arrived; L'Anse aux Meadows c.1000 only (no 1021 date)
errors.fix: Figures are roughly in line with the sagas and estimates; the only gap is the missing 1021 wood-cutting date, which is an omission, not an error.

errors.claim: Norse seafarers ranged roughly 6,000 km east to west
errors.fix: Newfoundland to Baghdad is closer to 8,000-9,000 km in a straight line, so 6,000 km is too low.

grade.best: It links geography, silver economics, political push and settlement limits into one causal chain explaining both how far the Vikings went and why they stopped, with the dirham hoards tied to the eastern route.
grade.worst: It should give the firm Iceland (c.870), Greenland (c.985) and L'Anse aux Meadows dates (wood cut in 1021) in one place, and correct the understated 6,000 km span.

errors.claim: Domestication on the Pontic-Caspian steppe (Botai herding c. 3500 BCE, the modern lineage c. 2200 BCE) fed the spoked-wheel chariot
errors.fix: Botai horses were not ancestors of the modern domestic horse (Librado 2021), so Botai does not belong in the lineage that fed the chariot; the answer frames it as one domestication sequence and places Botai on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, while Botai is in Kazakhstan.

errors.claim: Alexander's Companions rode without stirrups, and their xyston is called 'sarissa-style'
errors.fix: Lack of stirrups is correct; the xyston was a different, shorter lance than the infantry sarissa. Minor imprecision.

errors.claim: Darius III is said to have fielded scythed chariots, which failed against Alexander's disciplined infantry and Companion cavalry
errors.fix: Broadly accepted, but the scythed chariots failed mainly because Alexander's troops opened lanes and killed the crews; low-level imprecision.

errors.claim: Iron smelting at Kaman-Kalehöyük around 2000 BCE
errors.fix: Iron production at Kaman-Kalehöyük is dated to roughly 2000 BCE only for isolated early finds; widespread iron smelting there came much later (c. 1800-1200 BCE onward, with the Iron Age after 1200 BCE).

errors.claim: The chariot was a short phase between herding and cavalry, with cavalry only replacing it after chariots
errors.fix: Riding probably predates chariots (and Botai riding was possible), so 'between herding and cavalry' misstates the order; riding existed before and alongside the chariot.

grade.best: A clear causal chain from steppe grass to chariot cost to palace elites to brittle collapse to cheaper iron-age cavalry, with honest labelling of inference and dispute.
grade.worst: It never connects steppe migrations such as Yamnaya c. 3000 BCE to the spread of Indo-European languages, and it treats Botai and the chariot lineage as one sequence rather than clearly separate.

errors.claim: Hōkūle'a sailed Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 with Mau Piailug, a Micronesian navigator, using no instruments, 'showing the tradition works'
errors.fix: The claim is largely correct, but it shows that Pacific navigation methods work today, not that ancient navigators used them; the answer does hedge this.

errors.claim: Santa Cruz to Vanuatu to Fiji gaps of 350-900 km, and 'mostly downwind-ish' sailing in the western tropics
errors.fix: The eastward trip from the Bismarcks runs against the southeast trades; the answer contradicts itself on wind direction between steps 1 and 4.

errors.claim: Ancient DNA from Vanuatu and Tonga shows the earliest Lapita individuals were nearly all Austronesian-descended, 'a few canoes of 20-40 people each' and 'Lapita from Bismarcks over some 3,000 km'
errors.fix: The distance is inconsistent with the 4,000-4,500 km given elsewhere, and the canoe numbers are modelled estimates, which the answer admits.

grade.best: It builds a clear causal chain, with wind and current geometry explaining the long pause and navigation and possible climate windows explaining the later burst, and it honestly labels the climate trigger as unproven.
grade.worst: Voyaging technology is thin: the answer never names double-hulled voyaging canoes and treats navigation only in a scholar step, and it also has a messy wind-direction contradiction and a garbled Lipson citation.

errors.claim: Tikal fell to Calakmul's allies in 562, then in 695 Tikal's king Jasaw Chan K'awiil beat Calakmul
errors.fix: Tikal's defeat in 562 is correct, and the 695 victory is correct. No real error; but 'Dos Pilas ... about 100 km southwest of Tikal' is roughly right (about 110 km). Not an error.

grade.best: It builds a layered causal chain in which drought, dense populations on thin soil, failing divine kingship and escalating war interact, and it weighs Haug, Demarest and Diamond fairly with named unknowns.
grade.worst: Premise-checking is mostly implicit: it could state more directly that the collapse was regional and that the Maya people never disappeared, and it could add a clearer note that the Terminal Classic 'collapse' was uneven and non-uniform across cities.

points.note: Liverpool-Manchester 1830 named as the template and in step 10 as ordinary-people steam line, but 'first intercity, steam only' not stated

errors.claim: The Atlas dates railways to Stockton-on-Tees in 1825 and Manchester in 1830, with Liverpool-Manchester described as raw cotton going to mills 'in hours rather than a day or more by canal'
errors.fix: Plausible but loosely stated; not a clear error (minor).

errors.claim: Napoleon's Grande Armée reached the Danube around Ulm in about six weeks, then Vienna by mid-November, roughly 20-25 km/day sustained
errors.fix: Vienna was entered 13 November, plausible; but the Boulogne-to-Ulm march was about 500-700 km in ~6 weeks, which is consistent. No clear error.

errors.claim: Spain's broad gauge (1,668 mm) meant a change of trains at the Pyrenees, and the Orient Express in 1914 ran Paris to Constantinople in about three days averaging 900 km/day
errors.fix: Paris-Constantinople took around 2.5-3 days at roughly 1,000 km/day by direct route, but the 2,900 km figure and 'about 900 km a day' are rough; the Simplon Orient took about 68 hours. Acceptable rounding.

errors.claim: The Brenner railway (1867) made Vienna-to-Italy go from weeks of mule and coach to roughly a day
errors.fix: Brenner connected Innsbruck and Bozen/Verona; Vienna to Italy took more than a day by then, and the route to Italy from Vienna used the Semmering/Südbahn. Overstated.

errors.claim: Germany ran around 2,000 trains a day crossing the Rhine bridges at Cologne in 1914
errors.fix: About 2,000 trains a day across the Rhine overall in the first mobilization phase, with roughly 550 trains a day over Cologne bridges; the figure is exaggerated for Cologne alone.

grade.best: It gives a concrete, well-evidenced mechanism chain from speed to freight costs, armies, suburbs and emigration, and shows rail's limits at the railhead and in mountains.
grade.worst: It omits transcontinental lines (US 1869, Trans-Siberian) and railway time/time zones, and never states that Liverpool-Manchester was the first steam-only intercity line.

grade.best: It gives a clear, hedged abandonment account that weighs ecological strain against trade shift toward Mutapa and Khami, and openly says which factor weighed most is unsettled.
grade.worst: It barely addresses the colonial denial of African builders and the Rhodesian suppression of archaeologists, mentioning it only in passing as 'popular myths', and it misattributes Caton-Thompson as 'Gerald' with a loosely matched title.

points.reason: barays and canals on a flat plain, hydraulic city, but no lidar, ~1,000 km2 figure or low-density point in the steps; only the Evans/Fletcher view mentions lidar and low-density
Buckley tree rings, megadroughts then intense monsoon damaging the hydraulic system
1431 Ayutthaya sack, court moved to Phnom Penh and trade-facing seat
monks kept Angkor Wat, never fully empty (also in short and view)

errors.claim: Ayutthaya sits about 400 km west of Angkor, and Phnom Penh lies another 200 km southeast of Angkor
errors.fix: Ayutthaya is roughly 350-400 km west-northwest, fine; Phnom Penh is about 250 km southeast of Angkor, which contradicts the answer's own 250 km figure in step 5 (minor inconsistency)

errors.claim: Angkor sits 'a day or more from the lake'
errors.fix: The Tonlé Sap shore is only about 15-25 km from Angkor, a short haul (step 4 itself says 'short haul to the lake')

grade.best: It weighs climate, trade, Ayutthaya's pressure and politics as interacting causes with explicit hedging, and corrects the 'sudden abandonment' premise by noting the court moved and monks kept Angkor Wat.
grade.worst: State the lidar-based scale (about 1,000 km2 low-density urban sprawl) explicitly as the root of the system's vulnerability, and fix the inconsistent distances and the 'day or more from the lake' claim.

errors.claim: Between roughly 2600 and 1700 BCE the Indus cities shrank and urban life dissolved (frame), and the 'Madhav Possehl' attribution in step 11
errors.fix: The name is Gregory L. Possehl; 'Madhav Possehl' is a garbled name. The Mature phase ran about 2600-1900 BCE, with decline after.

errors.claim: tuberculosis, found at Indus sites like Lothal-era sites
errors.fix: Evidence of tuberculosis comes from Lothal and Harappa skeletal reports, but the phrasing is vague and the claim is weak.

errors.claim: Mohenjo-daro's 'massacre' skeletons were reinterpreted decades ago as scattered burials from different times
errors.fix: Broadly correct; but the answer says 'no destruction layer' with confidence, which is acceptable. No clear error.

grade.best: It states plainly what is and is not known, rejects the invasion myth with evidence (skeletons, Rakhigarhi DNA), and ties a gradual monsoon-driven decline to dispersal and crop diversification while flagging 100-200 year dating errors.
grade.worst: It never says directly that the Indus script is undeciphered and so no written account exists, and it names the 'best-supported driver' as monsoon weakening somewhat more firmly than the dating allows.

errors.claim: Columbus placed Japan about 3,700 km west of the Canaries, versus roughly 19,000 km in reality; also 'over ten thousand more' and Step 5 title 'Seven thousand versus twenty thousand'
errors.fix: Columbus's estimate was about 2,400 nautical miles (~4,400 km), and the true distance to Japan is about 10,600 nm (~19,600 km); the figures are inconsistent within the answer (3,700 km vs 2,400 nm vs 'seven thousand')

errors.claim: Portuguese advisers worked from a circumference near 40,000 km and al-Farghani's value gave about 20,400 km, implying medieval scholars inherited a ~20,000 km figure
errors.fix: Al-Farghani's 56 2/3 Arabic miles per degree gives a roughly accurate circumference; the ~20,400 km figure arises only when misread in shorter Italian miles, so presenting it as al-Farghani's circumference is misleading

errors.claim: Eratosthenes' result within 'a few percent to 15 percent'; Ptolemy shrank the degree to about 500 stadia and Columbus used Ptolemy's small Earth
errors.fix: Columbus relied mainly on Alfraganus and Marinus; Ptolemy's 500 stadia per degree is right, but attributing Columbus's small Earth to Ptolemy is loose

grade.best: It corrects the premise immediately and cleanly, showing the real dispute was Earth size and Asia's extent, that Columbus's critics were right, and that Irving and others manufactured the flat-Earth myth.
grade.worst: Clean up the inconsistent distance figures (3,700 km, 2,400 nm, 'seven thousand') and the muddled al-Farghani/Ptolemy numbers so the size argument is stated once, precisely.

errors.claim: Trotsky lived there from 1907 and edited the Pravda he published for Russian workers (Step 8); also Stalin lodged near Schönbrunn with Troyanovsky
errors.fix: Trotsky edited the Vienna Pravda (1908-1912) as a separate paper; it was not the Bolshevik St Petersburg Pravda. Stalin's stay with Troyanovsky is correct, but the claim that Trotsky's circle lodgings were on Schönbrunnerstraße is vague and uncertain.

errors.claim: Hitler was 'judged unfit when examined in Salzburg in 1914' and 'Hitler (aged 23)' in winter 1913
errors.fix: Hitler was 23 in early 1913 (born April 1889), which is correct; the Salzburg exam was Feb 1914, so this is fine. However, the claim that he lived in the Männerheim from Feb 1910 is correct, though he moved there in December 1909 to the Meldemannstraße in Feb 1910. This is a minor point.

errors.claim: Franz Joseph I aged 82 in one step and 83 in another; Trotsky was 'war correspondent in Balkans' so not at home
errors.fix: Franz Joseph turned 83 in August 1913, so both ages are possible. Trotsky did report on the Balkan Wars for Kievskaya Mysl in 1912-13, so this is reasonable.

errors.claim: Tito 'was a young metalworker in Croatia and later in Austria-Hungary's army' and Schoenberg 'moved to Berlin in 1911, returned, and ended in Los Angeles in 1933-34'
errors.fix: Tito worked in Wiener Neustadt in 1913, which the answer notes elsewhere. His army service began in 1913 after he was conscripted, so the description is loosely inconsistent.

grade.best: It clearly separates documented overlap (Hitler until May, Stalin for weeks) from legend, flagging the Café Central and Schönbrunn stories as unsupported and stating there is no evidence of a meeting.
grade.worst: It is too hedged about Trotsky (omitting that he edited Pravda in Vienna, conflating it with the Bolshevik paper) and about Tito's Wiener Neustadt work, and it repeats itself across steps.
